tur12-0: Peripheral Arterial Disease (Blocked Leg Arteries): Walking Exercise | İhsan Eren
tur12-1: Cramp-like calf pain when walking that eases after a few minutes’ rest? Peripheral arterial disease and claudication: symptoms, diagnosis, walking programme and warning signs.
tur12-2: Peripheral arterial disease: leg pain when walking, and exercise
tur12-3: Does a cramp-like pain start in your calf, thigh or buttock when you walk, and ease after a few minutes’ rest? Narrowing of the leg arteries can reduce the blood reaching your working muscles. This is called peripheral arterial disease, and the pain that comes on with walking is called intermittent claudication. Regular walking exercise clearly increases the distance you can walk without pain, and guidelines list it among the first steps of treatment.
tur12-6: Average increase in pain-free walking distance with exercise (Cochrane, 9 trials, 391 people)
tur12-8: Average increase in maximum walking distance (10 trials, 500 people)
tur12-10: Walking sessions of 30–60 minutes for at least 12 weeks (European Society of Cardiology consensus document)
tur12-12: People over 25 estimated to be living with peripheral arterial disease worldwide in 2015
tur12-13: Pain, cramp or tiredness in the calf, thigh or buttock that comes on when walking and eases after a few minutes’ rest.
tur12-14: Numbness or weakness in the legs.
tur12-15: Hair loss on the legs and feet; shiny, pale or bluish skin.
tur12-16: Brittle, slow-growing toenails; sores on the feet and legs that do not heal.
tur12-18: Many people with the condition have no symptoms at all. Recurring leg pain during exercise is not a normal part of ageing for someone who is otherwise healthy; you can see your doctor about it.
tur12-19: Who is more likely to get it?
tur12-20: People who smoke: this is the most important risk factor.
tur12-22: People with high blood pressure or high cholesterol.
tur12-23: It becomes more common with age: according to 2015 data, it affects 3.5–4.3% of people in their early 40s and 12–21% of people in their early 80s.
tur12-24: The narrowing is usually caused by fatty deposits building up in the artery wall (atherosclerosis). Because the same process can affect other arteries, people with peripheral arterial disease are also more likely to develop other cardiovascular diseases such as coronary heart disease, heart attack and stroke.
tur12-25: Your doctor will first ask about your symptoms and examine your legs and foot pulses. The most common test is the ankle–brachial pressure index (ABPI or ABI), which compares the blood pressure at your ankle with the blood pressure in your arm. According to the referral guidance of a Scottish health board, 0.9–1.4 is considered normal; below 0.9 suggests narrowed arteries and below 0.5 suggests severe narrowing. In people with diabetes or advanced kidney disease and in the very elderly, stiff artery walls can make the value misleadingly high.
tur12-26: Arteries are not the only cause of leg pain when walking. Lumbar spinal stenosis can also cause leg pain on walking, but this pain usually eases when you sit down or lean forward, and even standing can bring it on. For short cramps that wake you at night, see the night leg cramps guide.
tur12-27: A 2017 Cochrane review looked at 32 randomised controlled trials involving 1,835 people. Compared with usual care, exercise increased pain-free walking distance by an average of 82 metres and maximum walking distance by an average of 120 metres; these results are based on high-quality evidence, and the gains lasted for up to 2 years. Exercise did not change the ankle–brachial pressure index; no effect on death or amputation could be shown, while quality of life may improve.
tur12-28: How hard you walk also seems to matter. In the LITE trial of 305 people in the USA, participants walked at home 5 times a week for 12 months, for up to 50 minutes per session. Those who walked at a pace that caused moderate to severe leg pain increased their 6-minute walk distance by 34.5 metres; those who walked at a comfortable pace that caused no pain did not improve, and their results did not differ from the group that did no exercise.
tur12-29: The European Society of Cardiology’s 2024 consensus document sees supervised walking exercise as first-line treatment: at least 3 sessions a week, at least 30 minutes per session, for at least 3 months. Because pain can make it hard to keep going, the document recommends a flexible, person-centred approach: start at a light-to-moderate intensity and increase it as tolerated.
tur12-30: How to do the walking programme
tur12-32: Talk to your doctor before you start. If you have heart disease, your cardiologist may ask for an exercise stress test.
tur12-33: Start by walking at a slow pace for a few minutes.
tur12-35: Walk until the pain in your leg reaches a moderate to severe level.
tur12-37: Stop until the pain has gone completely, then start walking again.
tur12-39: Keep up the walk–rest cycle until your total time is up. England’s NHS recommends at least 30 minutes, several times a week; the European document describes starting at around 20 minutes and working up towards 60 minutes.
tur12-41: Use a step counter, a phone app or a simple walking diary. Monitored home programmes work better than unmonitored ones.
tur12-43: Do not stop walking when the programme ends; the benefit fades once regular exercise stops.
tur12-44: To set your steps to a steady pace, you can use the brisk walking metronome.
tur12-45: Six movements to go with your walking
tur12-46: Interval walking is the core of the programme. The other movements are for strengthening your leg muscles, warming up or for days when you cannot go out for a walk; the choice of strength exercises and the numbers of repetitions are general recommendations. Stop at once if you get chest pain, dizziness or unusual shortness of breath.
tur12-47: Warm up at a slow pace for a few minutes. Then walk until the pain in your leg reaches a moderate to severe level, stop and rest until the pain goes, then walk again. Repeat the walk–rest cycle until your total time is up.
tur12-48: Start with 20–30 minutes, aim for 30–60 minutes; at least 3 days a week
tur12-50: When the weather is bad, or to warm up before a walk: sit upright on a sturdy chair, lift and lower your knees in turn and swing your arms as well.
tur12-52: Hold lightly on to a kitchen worktop. Lift both heels together to rise up on to your toes, then lower slowly. This strengthens your calf muscles.
tur12-53: Sit at the front of a sturdy chair. Stand up as you breathe out, and sit down slowly as you breathe in. Use your hands for support if you need to.
tur12-54: Sit upright on a chair. Slowly straighten your knee and tighten the muscle at the front of your thigh, hold for 3 seconds and lower. As it gets easier, you can add a light weight at your ankle.
tur12-56: Holding the banister, climb a few stairs and come down slowly. If pain starts, stop and rest, then carry on once it has passed.
tur12-57: 1–3 flights, a few times a day
tur12-59: Reduces the risk of the condition getting worse and the risk of serious events such as heart attack.
tur12-60: Your doctor may recommend a cholesterol-lowering medicine (statin), medicines that reduce blood clotting and blood pressure medicines. For people with diabetes, blood sugar control also matters.
tur12-62: NICE recommends balloon angioplasty only when advice on risk factors has been followed, a supervised exercise programme has not brought enough improvement and imaging shows that the procedure is suitable. Bypass surgery is another option.
tur12-63: Is it harmful to keep walking through the pain?
tur12-64: No. This pain comes from the working muscles not getting enough blood, and it eases with rest. England’s NICE guideline recommends walking to the point of maximal pain, and the European Society of Cardiology’s consensus document recommends walking until the pain is moderate to severe; pain-free walking also improves walking to some extent, but the evidence for it is weaker. Pain that continues at rest, or a sudden change in the leg, is a different matter; see the warning signs below.
tur12-65: Does walking unblock the narrowed artery?
tur12-66: In studies, exercise did not change the ankle–brachial pressure index (a measure of arterial narrowing). The gain is in how far you can walk and in daily life. Stopping smoking and the medicines your doctor recommends are also important for slowing the narrowing.
tur12-68: NICE recommends a supervised exercise programme for everyone with intermittent claudication: about 2 hours a week for 3 months. If you cannot find such a programme, a structured home programme is a good option. According to the European Society of Cardiology’s document, home programmes monitored with a step counter, a walking diary or regular phone calls give results close to supervised programmes, while unmonitored programmes are less effective. The US guideline also recommends structured programmes that include support for behaviour change; the benefit of unplanned, casual walking is uncertain.
tur12-69: Programmes usually last at least 12 weeks. In the studies in the Cochrane review, exercise programmes were mostly done at least twice a week for 3 to 12 months, and the gains lasted up to 2 years. The benefit fades when you stop exercising, so it is important to keep walking regularly after the programme ends.
tur12-70: What can I do if I cannot walk?
tur12-71: According to the European and US guidelines, walking is the first choice; if walking is not possible, cycling, arm cycling (arm ergometry) or strength exercises can also be used. Walking usually increases walking distance more than strength exercises do, while cycling and arm cycling stand out for improving heart and lung fitness.
tur12-72: Why does smoking matter so much?
tur12-73: Smoking is the most important risk factor for peripheral arterial disease. Stopping reduces the risk of the condition getting worse and of other serious cardiovascular events such as heart attack. People who keep smoking after diagnosis have a much higher risk of heart attack.
tur12-74: For exercise after a heart attack or bypass surgery, see the cardiac rehabilitation guide; for nerve damage in the feet from diabetes, see the diabetic neuropathy guide.
tur12-75: For the situations marked “emergency”, call 112 or go to the nearest emergency department:
tur12-76: Sudden pain, coldness, paleness, numbness or weakness in your leg or arm: this may be a sudden blockage of an artery (emergency)
tur12-77: Foot or toe pain that continues at rest, gets worse especially at night and eases when you hang your leg over the side of the bed (see a doctor as soon as possible)
tur12-78: A sore below the knee that has not healed for more than 2 weeks, or a toe turning black
tur12-79: Chest pain, pressure or unusual shortness of breath while walking: stop exercising and see your doctor

tur12-90: Concussion after a blow to the head: emergency signs, what to do in the first 24–48 hours, a six-stage return to school, work and sport, balance exercises and the evidence.
tur12-91: Concussion: recovery and a gradual return to activity
tur12-92: Do you have a headache, dizziness, a dazed feeling or trouble concentrating after a blow to the head, a fall or a sudden jolt? Concussion is an injury in which the brain is temporarily affected. Symptoms usually clear within a few days to a few weeks. The long, strict rest that used to be advised is no longer recommended: after 24–48 hours of relative rest, returning step by step to everyday tasks and light activity helps recovery.
tur12-93: Relative rest, then a gradual return to light activity
tur12-95: Earliest return to competitive sport (UK grassroots sport guidelines)
tur12-97: Average recovery time in young people doing light aerobic exercise vs stretching only
tur12-99: If dizziness, neck pain or headache lasts longer than this, neck and balance rehabilitation is recommended
tur12-101: If any of the following apply after a blow to the head, get medical help straight away rather than using this guide. Do not drive yourself to the emergency department.
tur12-103: The person was knocked out and has not woken up, or is struggling to stay awake
tur12-105: They have difficulty speaking, understanding, walking or keeping their balance, or numbness or weakness in part of the body
tur12-106: They have problems with their vision or hearing
tur12-107: Clear fluid or blood is coming from the ears or nose, or there is bruising behind the ears
tur12-108: They fell from more than 1 metre or 5 stairs, or were hit at speed, such as in a car or bike accident
tur12-110: The person was knocked out briefly but has woken up
tur12-111: They have vomited, or keep vomiting
tur12-112: They have a headache that painkillers do not ease, or that keeps getting worse
tur12-113: They have memory problems, increasing drowsiness, irritability or a change in behaviour; a baby or young child is crying more than usual
tur12-114: They take blood-thinning medicine, have a bleeding disorder or have had brain surgery
tur12-115: They had alcohol or drugs just before the injury
tur12-117: Feeling dazed or “foggy”, difficulty concentrating and remembering.
tur12-118: Sensitivity to light or noise, tiredness, changes in sleep.
tur12-119: Changes in mood, such as irritability, anxiety or tearfulness.
tur12-120: Symptoms usually start within 24 hours, but can be delayed by up to 3 weeks. Mild symptoms can last up to 2 weeks; most people recover within 4 weeks.
tur12-122: Have an adult with you for the first 24 hours; do not stay on your own.
tur12-123: Rest and sleep as much as you need; keep phone, computer and screen time to a minimum.
tur12-124: Do not drink alcohol; do not take sleeping pills unless your doctor recommends them.
tur12-125: Do not ride a bicycle or operate machinery for the first 24 hours; do not drive until you have fully recovered.
tur12-126: For a headache you can take paracetamol or ibuprofen at the dose on the packet; you can hold ice wrapped in a towel to any swelling.
tur12-127: A gradual return to activity and sport
tur12-128: The UK guidelines for grassroots sport, produced with government support, describe the return in six stages. It is fine for your symptoms to rise slightly as you move on to the next stage, as long as the activity makes them no more than mildly worse and the increase settles within minutes to a few hours. If symptoms get clearly worse, go back to the previous stage.
tur12-130: First 24–48 hours: calm activities, minimal screen time.
tur12-132: Short, easy reading, short walks, light household tasks.
tur12-134: Mental tasks in blocks of 20–30 minutes; 10–15 minutes of light aerobic exercise (walking, exercise bike).
tur12-135: 4. Part-time school or work, non-contact training
tur12-136: Once you have no symptoms at rest, usually around week 2.
tur12-137: 5. Full-time school or work, unrestricted training
tur12-138: Day 15 at the earliest; after 14 days without symptoms at rest.
tur12-140: Not before day 21; after 14 days without symptoms at rest.
tur12-141: Returning to school or work comes before returning to sport. The guidelines’ principle is clear: if in doubt, sit them out. Someone with suspected concussion does not go back to the game, training or PE that day, and stays away from them for at least 24 hours.
tur12-142: According to the international consensus agreed in Amsterdam in 2022 and published in 2023, strict rest is not recommended; everyday tasks and light aerobic exercise such as walking or an exercise bike may help recovery, and limiting screen time in the first 48 hours may also help. The consensus recommends neck and balance rehabilitation for people whose dizziness, neck pain or headache lasts longer than 10 days, and an assessment involving different specialties for those whose symptoms last more than 4 weeks.
tur12-143: One of the studies behind these recommendations involved 103 young athletes in the USA: those who did about 20 minutes of aerobic exercise a day within the first 10 days, at an intensity that did not worsen their symptoms (80% of the heart rate at which symptoms increased on a treadmill test), recovered in an average of 13 days, compared with 17 days for those who only stretched. Recovery took longer than 4 weeks for 2 of 52 people in the exercise group and 7 of 51 in the stretching group, but this difference was not statistically significant. The studies were mostly done in young athletes; evidence in adults and in injuries outside sport is more limited.
tur12-144: Six exercises for light movement and balance
tur12-145: These movements are started in stages 2 and 3, after the rest period. The head movement and balance exercises come from a children’s hospital information sheet on balance after concussion. Each movement should make your symptoms no more than mildly worse; if dizziness persists or you are afraid of falling, get checked by a physiotherapist or doctor.
tur12-147: Walk at a comfortable pace on a flat route. If your symptoms rise no more than slightly and settle quickly, you can make the walk a little longer each day.
tur12-148: Start with a few minutes; 10–15 minutes in stage 3
tur12-150: Hold a pen or a card at arm’s length and keep your eyes on it. With your eyes locked on the object, slowly turn your head from side to side. Only speed up when you are ready.
tur12-153: Sit upright. Slowly lift your head to look at the ceiling, then lower it to look at the floor. The aim is to help your brain get used to head movement again; any dizziness should stay mild and pass quickly.
tur12-154: Sit upright. Slowly bring your ear towards your shoulder, come back to the middle and tilt to the other side. Do not lift your shoulder.
tur12-157: Stand next to a wall. First stand for 10 seconds with one foot slightly in front of the other, then swap feet. When this gets easier, walk along a corridor heel to toe, touching the heel to the toes of the front foot.
tur12-158: 10 seconds with each foot in front; then 20 steps
tur12-160: Holding a sturdy chair, stand on one leg. When it gets easier, let go and hold for longer; later you can make it harder, for example by closing your eyes or drawing letters in the air.
tur12-161: Start with 10 seconds, up to 30 seconds
tur12-162: Don’t I need to rest in a dark room?
tur12-163: No. Long, strict rest is no longer recommended. In a study of 88 patients aged 11–22, those told to rest completely at home for 5 days reported more symptoms, and their symptoms cleared more slowly, than those who rested for 1–2 days and then gradually returned to activity. Rest relatively for the first 24–48 hours and sleep as much as you can; then gradually return to everyday tasks and gentle walks.
tur12-164: Can I use my phone and computer?
tur12-165: Keeping screen time to a minimum in the first 48 hours may help recovery. After that you can use screens for short periods with breaks; in stage 3, mental tasks are recommended in blocks of 20–30 minutes.
tur12-166: When can I go back to school or work?
tur12-167: When you feel better, starting with short periods. The UK grassroots sport guidelines put the return to school and work before the return to sport: once you have no symptoms at rest, usually around week 2, you can go back to school or work part-time. During this time you can ask for adjustments such as extra time for homework and exams.
tur12-168: You return to training gradually; you do not return to contact or competitive sport before day 21 after the injury, and you need to have been free of symptoms at rest for at least 14 days. The NHS also advises staying away from contact sports for at least 3 weeks. Children should avoid rough play for the first few days. According to the international consensus, most people are fully back in their sport within about a month.
tur12-170: Light aerobic exercise may help. In a study of 103 young people aged 13–18 with sport-related concussion, those who started within the first 10 days and walked or used an exercise bike for about 20 minutes a day, at an intensity that did not worsen their symptoms, recovered in an average of 13 days; for those who only stretched, it took 17 days. The intensity should stay at a level that makes your symptoms no more than mildly worse.
tur12-171: What should I do if my symptoms don’t go away?
tur12-172: See your doctor if symptoms have not improved within 2 weeks or are getting worse; if they last more than 4 weeks, an assessment involving different specialties is recommended. If dizziness, neck pain or headache lasts longer than 10 days, the international consensus recommends neck and balance (cervicovestibular) rehabilitation. In a small study of 31 people aged 12–30 with sport-related concussion, 73% of those who had this rehabilitation were cleared to return to sport within 8 weeks, compared with 7% of those who had usual care only.
tur12-173: For neck pain after a blow to the head, see the whiplash guide; for headache, the headache guide; for brief spinning that starts when you turn your head, the dizziness (BPPV) guide.
tur12-174: Your symptoms are getting worse or have not improved within 2 weeks
tur12-175: You are unsure whether it is safe to drive or go back to work, school or sport
tur12-176: Your symptoms last longer than 4 weeks: do not return to sport until you have been assessed
tur12-177: If any of the emergency signs above appear later, call 112 or go to the emergency department straight away

tur12-186: Pelvic Organ Prolapse (Womb Prolapse): Symptoms and Pelvic Floor Exercises | İhsan Eren
tur12-187: A heavy or dragging feeling in the vagina: symptoms and types of pelvic organ prolapse, pelvic floor exercises, pessaries, everyday tips and what the evidence says.
tur12-188: Pelvic organ prolapse (prolapse of the womb, bladder or bowel)
tur12-189: Do you have a feeling of heaviness in your lower tummy, a sense of something coming down in your vagina, or a feeling like sitting on a small ball? The womb, bladder or bowel can slip down from their normal position and bulge into the wall of the vagina. This is very common and is not life-threatening. For mild and moderate prolapse, the first treatment option is pelvic floor exercise with a physiotherapist for at least 16 weeks; small changes to everyday habits can also ease symptoms.
tur12-190: Approximate proportion of women worldwide who will experience pelvic organ prolapse at some point in their lives
tur12-192: Minimum length of supervised pelvic floor training, the first option for stage 1–2 prolapse (NICE)
tur12-194: Women saying their prolapse was better at 12 months: exercise group vs leaflet group (POPPY)
tur12-195: Home exercise frequency aimed for in POPPY
tur12-196: A feeling of heaviness in the lower tummy or genital area.
tur12-197: A dragging feeling in the vagina, a sense of something coming down; feeling like sitting on a small ball.
tur12-198: A bulge in the vagina that you can see or feel.
tur12-199: Not emptying your bladder fully, needing to pass urine often, leaking urine when you cough or sneeze.
tur12-202: Some women have no symptoms at all; the prolapse is found during an examination done for another reason.
tur12-204: Front wall prolapse: the bladder bulges into the front wall of the vagina.
tur12-205: Back wall prolapse: the bowel bulges into the back wall of the vagina.
tur12-206: Uterine prolapse: the womb comes down into the vagina.
tur12-207: Vault prolapse: after a hysterectomy, the top of the vagina sags down.
tur12-208: These can happen together; severity is usually graded from 1 (mild) to 4 (severe). Pregnancy and childbirth (especially a long or difficult birth, a large baby or a multiple birth), ageing and the menopause, being overweight, long-term constipation or coughing, having a hysterectomy and jobs involving heavy lifting all raise the risk. Conditions affecting connective tissue, such as joint hypermobility, can also raise the risk.
tur12-209: What can you do in everyday life?
tur12-210: Eat plenty of vegetables, fruit and fibre, and drink 1.5–2 litres of fluid a day. On the toilet, put your feet on a footstool so that your knees are higher than your hips; rest your elbows on your knees, breathe out and do not strain.
tur12-212: Do not strain when passing urine; to empty fully, you can lean forward gently a few times.
tur12-214: Split loads into lighter parts and carry them in several trips; think about how often you do repeated lifting tasks too.
tur12-216: Extra weight increases the load on the pelvic floor. NICE recommends losing weight if your body mass index is over 30.
tur12-217: Get a cough treated, stop smoking
tur12-218: A long-lasting cough strains the pelvic floor again and again; stopping smoking lowers the risk of a cough.
tur12-219: Break up long periods of standing
tur12-220: Sit down and rest every so often during the day.
tur12-221: In POPPY, the largest trial, 447 women with newly diagnosed, symptomatic stage 1–3 prolapse were divided into two groups. One group was taught individualised pelvic floor exercises in 5 sessions over 16 weeks; at home they aimed for ten 10-second contractions and up to 50 fast contractions three times a day, and also practised tightening the muscles before moments of strain (“the knack”). The other group was given only a lifestyle leaflet. At 12 months, the prolapse symptom score had fallen more in the exercise group (an average of 3.77 vs 2.09 points), and 57% vs 45% said their prolapse was better.
tur12-222: The Cochrane review included four trials (857 women) comparing pelvic floor exercise with no treatment. All the trials that reported symptoms favoured exercise; in the combined result of two trials, exercise increased the chance of the prolapse stage improving by 17%. Some of the trials were small and at risk of bias.
tur12-223: Working the pelvic floor muscles correctly is not easy at first. If you cannot feel the muscles, or the exercises make your symptoms worse, you can ask for an assessment by a physiotherapist who works in pelvic health.
tur12-224: Six exercises for the pelvic floor
tur12-225: The target doses for the first four exercises come from the home programme in the POPPY trial. It is normal to start with less; hold for as long as you can and build up over the weeks. For a tool that guides you second by second, you can use the pelvic floor timer.
tur12-227: Lie on your back with your knees bent. Draw your pelvic floor muscles in and up as if holding in wind and urine at the same time, squeeze as strongly as you can and hold, then relax fully. Do not hold your breath; do not squeeze your buttocks or tummy.
tur12-228: Target: ten 10-second squeezes, three times a day
tur12-230: Sit upright. Squeeze the same muscles quickly and let go straight away. Fast squeezes help the muscles switch on quickly during sudden strains such as a cough or sneeze.
tur12-231: Target: up to 50 fast squeezes, three times a day
tur12-233: Once you can do them easily lying down and sitting, try the squeezes standing up too. You can do them while washing up or waiting in a queue.
tur12-234: Long and fast squeezes, three times a day
tur12-236: Just before you cough, sneeze, laugh or lift something, squeeze your pelvic floor muscles and hold until the movement is over. This lets the muscles give support when pressure inside the tummy rises.
tur12-238: If you have to lift something, squeeze your pelvic floor first, keep the load close to your body and do not hold your breath; breathe out as you lift. Split heavy loads into lighter parts and carry them in several trips.
tur12-241: Instead of activities where both feet leave the ground, such as running, jumping and trampolining, you can choose lower-impact exercise such as brisk walking, cycling, swimming, Pilates or a cross-trainer.
tur12-243: Will pelvic floor exercises cure my prolapse?
tur12-244: They can ease the symptoms. In the POPPY trial of 447 women in the UK, New Zealand and Australia, women who did 5 sessions of pelvic floor exercise with a physiotherapist over 16 weeks had a greater reduction in prolapse symptoms than those who received only an information leaflet. At 12 months, 57% in the exercise group and 45% in the leaflet group said their prolapse was better. The difference was significant but modest. In the Cochrane review, pelvic floor exercise also increased the chance of the prolapse stage improving by 17% compared with no exercise.
tur12-245: How long should I keep exercising?
tur12-246: For stage 1–2 prolapse, NICE recommends supervised pelvic floor training lasting at least 16 weeks as the first option, and asks that it be continued afterwards if the programme helps. Muscles take time to get stronger; keep going regularly even if you do not notice a difference in the first weeks.
tur12-247: What is a pessary, and who is it for?
tur12-248: A pessary is a plastic or silicone ring placed in the vagina to support the organs. NICE says it can be considered for symptomatic prolapse, on its own or together with pelvic floor exercises. More than one fitting may be needed to find the right size, and the pessary should be removed at least every 6 months. In the TOPSY trial of 340 women, women who learned to remove and insert their own pessary had a similar quality of life to those cared for in clinic, and reported fewer problems.
tur12-249: Surgery may be offered to women whose symptoms have not improved with non-surgical treatment, or who do not want it. The decision can be made together with your doctor, after talking through the options, expected benefits, risks and the chance of the prolapse coming back. In England’s National Health Service (NHS), operations placing mesh inside the vagina are no longer done unless there is no other option.
tur12-251: Yes, staying active matters. If your pelvic floor muscles are weak, high-impact activities such as running, jumping and trampolining can make symptoms worse; lower-impact exercise such as brisk walking, cycling, swimming and Pilates are good choices. Cut down on heavy lifting as much as you can.
tur12-252: Why did it get worse after the menopause?
tur12-253: Ageing and the menopause are among the risk factors for prolapse. Women with symptoms related to the menopause, such as vaginal dryness and irritation, may be offered oestrogen used inside the vagina as a cream, tablet or ring; it can also be considered before starting a pessary. You can talk to your doctor about this.
tur12-254: For leaking urine when you cough or feel a sudden urge, see the urinary incontinence guide; for the tummy muscles after childbirth, see the tummy muscle separation guide.

tur12-265: Muscle strengthening 2 days a week: a 4- or 6-exercise home circuit with body weight and a resistance band, a work–rest timer with sound, weekly tracking and the evidence.
tur12-267: You do not need a gym to strengthen your muscles. This timer takes you through a circuit of four or six exercises at home, using your body weight and a resistance band: it counts the work and rest time for each exercise and shows you what comes next. The World Health Organization recommends muscle-strengthening exercise on at least 2 days a week; the timer also counts your days this week.

tur12-277: Choose the number of exercises, the work time and the number of rounds. During the work time, repeat the exercise at a controlled pace; during the rest time, get ready for the next exercise. If your sound is on you will hear a beep at each change; if you like, the names of the exercises are read out too.
tur12-286: Sit at the front of a sturdy chair without arms. Stand up without using your hands, then sit down slowly. If it is too hard, put your hands on your knees for support.
tur12-287: Place your hands on the wall at chest height. Keeping your elbows close to your body, bend them to bring your chest towards the wall, then push back. As it gets easier, you can move to a kitchen worktop and later to a low table.
tur12-288: Anchor the band to a door handle or under your feet. Keeping your elbows close to your body, pull the band towards you, squeeze your shoulder blades together and release slowly. If you have no band, squeeze your shoulder blades together and hold for a few seconds.
tur12-290: Holding the banister, step up on to the bottom stair, or on to a sturdy, low step, one foot at a time, and step down. Halfway through, switch the leading foot.
tur12-291: Lie on your back with your knees bent and feet on the floor. Squeeze your buttocks and lift your hips off the floor so that your shoulders and knees form a straight line. Lower slowly.
tur12-292: Hold lightly on to a kitchen worktop or the back of a chair. Lift both heels together to rise up on to your toes, then lower slowly. When it gets easier, try without holding on.

tur12-311: In the first weeks, start with 4 exercises and 1 round, and build up gradually.

tur12-316: Mild muscle tiredness is normal; if you get sharp joint pain, skip that exercise.
tur12-318: The World Health Organization recommends that everyone over 18 does, alongside at least 150 minutes of moderate-intensity activity a week, strengthening exercises working the major muscle groups on at least 2 days a week. This circuit works the muscles of the legs, hips, chest, arms and back together.
tur12-320: In a meta-analysis combining 16 observational studies, people who did muscle-strengthening exercise had a 10–17% lower risk of death, cardiovascular disease, cancer, diabetes and lung cancer. For death, cardiovascular disease and cancer, the largest reduction was seen at about 30–60 minutes a week; well beyond that, no clear extra benefit was seen. People who combined strengthening with aerobic exercise had a 40% lower risk of death. These studies show associations; they do not prove cause and effect.
tur12-322: In a randomised trial of 97 people over 65 at Penn State University in the USA, published in PLOS One in 2026, participants did a programme of about 4 minutes every day: press-ups, chair stands, rows with a resistance band and step-ups; each exercise for 30 seconds, followed by 30 seconds’ rest. Compared with the group that did no exercise, the programme increased the number of chair stands in 30 seconds by 4.2 and the time standing on one leg by 3.6 seconds. Participants did the programme on 81% of days.
tur12-323: Do I need to use weights?
tur12-324: Not to get started. In a 2023 analysis combining 178 studies, every form of resistance exercise studied increased muscle strength and muscle size compared with no exercise. The biggest gains in strength, however, came with heavier loads and more than one set. You can start with your body weight and a resistance band and make the exercises harder as they get easier.
tur12-325: When should I make it harder?
tur12-326: If at the end of the work time you feel you could still do a few more repetitions, you can make the exercise harder: press-ups on a worktop instead of the wall, a stronger band, heel raises without holding on, or a single-leg bridge. Slowly increasing the number of repetitions is another way.
tur12-328: If you have heart disease or uncontrolled high blood pressure, have had recent surgery, or your doctor has restricted exercise, check with them first. Do not hold your breath while exercising; stop if you get chest pain, dizziness or sharp joint pain.

tur12-337: You do not need a treadmill or a long corridor to measure your fitness. You step on the spot for 2 minutes and count how many times your right knee reaches a set height. This page keeps the time, helps you count the steps and, for ages 60–94, compares your result with people your age and with a threshold linked to staying independent in later life.

tur12-381: Your aerobic endurance: the fitness you need to walk, climb stairs and carry on with daily tasks without tiring. It is part of the Senior Fitness Test, developed for people over 60; because it does not need a long walking space, it can also be done at home. In small studies, its results agreed well with the time to walk 1 mile (about 1.6 km) and with a treadmill test.
tur12-382: How high should I lift my knee?
tur12-383: To halfway between the middle of your kneecap and the highest point of your hip bone (the top of the pelvis). Find this height with a tape measure while standing, and mark it on the wall beside you with a piece of tape. Only steps in which your right knee reaches this mark are counted.
tur12-384: Can I hold on to something?
tur12-385: Yes. If your balance is not good, you can hold on to a wall, a table or the back of a chair. For safety, have someone with you; they can count the steps too.
tur12-386: Where do the values come from?
tur12-387: The ranges in the table show the middle half (25th to 75th percentile) of people your age, from values obtained from 7,183 people aged 60–94 in the USA. The independence thresholds were published by the same researchers in 2013 and aim at the fitness needed to keep living independently into your 90s. Because these thresholds were set taking expected future decline into account, they are slightly above average in the younger age groups.
tur12-388: I am under 60 – what does my result show?
tur12-389: The comparison values for this test are for ages 60–94. If you are younger, you can save your result and repeat the test every few weeks to track your own progress.
tur12-390: How can I improve my result?
tur12-391: With regular aerobic activity: the World Health Organization recommends at least 150 minutes of moderate-intensity activity a week, and brisk walking is the easiest way to get it. Strengthening your leg muscles also helps. Repeat the test every few weeks under the same conditions; small one-off differences may be measurement error, so look at the trend.

tur12-397: Supervised exercise for ongoing knee problems after ACL reconstruction: safe, with a modest benefit
tur12-398: The average effect of exercise in hip osteoarthritis is smaller than expected: a Cochrane update
tur12-399: A 4-minute daily strength workout improved leg strength and balance in people over 65
tur12-400: The SUPER-Knee trial, run by La Trobe University in Australia and published in Annals of Internal Medicine on 29 September 2026, included 184 people aged 18–40 who still had knee problems 9–36 months after anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) reconstruction. Half received 4 months of progressive exercise and education supervised by a physiotherapist; the other half received a single education session and resources for exercising on their own. At 4 months, the knee symptom and function score (KOOS4, 0–100) improved by 14.1 points in the supervised group and 9.4 points in the other group; the difference was 4.8 points. Meaningful pain improvement was reported by 73% vs 40%, and thigh muscle strength increased more in the supervised group. On MRI, no difference was seen between the groups in cartilage thickness or composition at 4 and 12 months.
tur12-401: The difference was modest, and it narrowed by 12 months because the control group also kept improving. The trial was not blinded; participants knew which group they were in, and most outcomes were self-reported. Young adults who have had ACL reconstruction are at risk of early knee osteoarthritis; in this trial there was no sign that intensive exercise harmed the cartilage.
tur12-402: Sources: Annals of Internal Medicine, 29 September 2026 · News-Medical, 29 September 2026 · Medical Dialogues, 5 October 2026
tur12-404: A Cochrane review published on 23 July 2026 by researchers from the universities of Sydney and Melbourne looked at 18 trials involving 1,368 people with hip osteoarthritis; programmes lasted 2 to 52 weeks and included strengthening, aerobic and mind–body exercise. Compared with no treatment, usual care or education alone, exercise improved pain by an average of 7.2 points and function by 8.8 points on a 100-point scale, whereas an improvement of about 12–13 points is generally considered necessary for a person to notice it in daily life. Compared with a sham treatment, exercise had little or no effect on pain; exercise added to another treatment did not clearly change pain or function either. There was no meaningful improvement in quality of life.
tur12-405: This does not mean exercise does not work: the authors stress that exercise should continue to be recommended as a core treatment for hip osteoarthritis, and that it is cheap and unlikely to cause harm. But they say patients should be given realistic expectations, and that larger studies are needed to show who benefits from which kind of exercise. Most trials were small, participants knew which group they were in, and 63% of participants were women aged 53 to 74.
tur12-406: Sources: Cochrane Library, 23 July 2026 · Cochrane plain language summary · University of Sydney, 23 July 2026
tur12-408: In the FAST-2 trial, published in PLOS One in 2026 by researchers at Penn State College of Medicine in the USA, 97 people with an average age of 74 who exercised for only about 18 minutes a week on average were randomly divided into two groups. The exercise group did a programme of about 4 minutes every day: press-ups, chair stands, rows with a resistance band and step-ups; each exercise for 30 seconds, followed by 30 seconds’ rest. Participants were given resistance bands and a height-adjustable step, and the exercises were made harder as they got stronger. Compared with the group that did no exercise, the number of chair stands in 30 seconds increased by 4.2, the time standing on one leg by 3.6 seconds, and sit-to-stand became 2.3 seconds faster. Participants did the programme on 81% of days.
tur12-409: The press coverage does not give the groups’ starting and final values or confidence intervals, and the claim in some headlines that the programme “quadrupled fitness” is not supported by the figures given. Still, the result is randomised evidence that short but daily strengthening can work in older people. To do a similar circuit at home, you can use the strength circuit in the Look after yourself section.
tur12-410: Sources: PLOS One, 2026 · Penn State, 9 June 2026 · Penn State Health News, 12 June 2026
